32.0: One should always be shrewd in their fear of Heaven, responding gently and increasing peace with one's brethren and relatives, so that they will be loved above (by God) and pleasant below (to others), and accepted by all creatures. This applies even to a non-Jew in the marketplace, meaning a non-Jew who does not know him personally but happens to encounter him in the marketplace. How much more so when the non-Jew knows him. It was said about Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai that he never failed to greet anyone with peace, even a non-Jew in the marketplace.

74.3: Regarding terumah (priestly offerings), one does not change food into a liquid except for olives and grapes alone. Based on this, dates that are terumah should not be made into beer, nor should honey be made from them. Similarly, beer should not be made from apples, nor vinegar from late-season grapes. Late-season grapes are those that remain attached to the vine until autumn because their nature is such that they do not ripen until that time. These grapes are suitable only for vinegar, not for wine. Likewise, for all other fruits, one does not convert them from a solid state into a liquid, as their extracted liquid is considered mere moisture and not significant enough to be classified as terumah—except for olives and grapes, as explained. Nevertheless, if the liquid was already extracted, one may drink it while maintaining the purity of terumah. If someone drinks it unknowingly (without realizing it was terumah), they are exempt even from repaying the principal amount, and certainly, they are not required to add the usual fifth. This ruling has already been written in Tractate Chullin.
74.4: However, one may crush a terumah fruit or cut it into small pieces with a knife without concern.
